title: AI makes more unpaid work, firing up unions
full_text:
Artificial intelligence has failed to reduce workloads for more than three-quarters of Australian workers, including one in eight whose unpaid overtime has increased since the technology was introduced, a new national survey of more than 6600 workers has found.
Unions NSW, which commissioned the survey, is calling for new “guardrails” around AI use, and is discussing with affiliates making applications to the Fair Work Commission to vary awards to ensure workers are properly compensated when performing overtime.
Examining the prevalence of unpaid overtime in Australian workplaces, with a focus on the impacts of AI, the survey found 63 per cent had seen no change in unpaid overtime following the introduction of AI, while 13 per cent were now working more overtime without pay.
One in five workers said employers expected higher output as a direct result of AI integration. About one quarter of workers believed their job could be replaced by AI within the next five years, and concerns were significantly higher among younger workers.
“Tech companies hype AI as a way to reduce workloads, but the evidence shows that any productivity gains are being absorbed into higher performance expectations, tighter deadlines, and expanding job scope,” incoming Unions NSW secretary Thomas Costa told The Australian.
“Rather than easing the burden on workers, employers are increasingly using AI to extract more from their workers, faster, longer and often unpaid.” Unpaid overtime was becoming entrenched as a new normal for Australian workers, with 88 per cent regularly working beyond their paid hours, an increase of two percentage points since the last survey in 2024.
Workers are giving away an average of 7.8 hours of unpaid labour every week, equivalent to more than 11 weeks of unpaid work each year and almost $22,000 in lost wages.
Mr Costa, who formally succeeds Mark Morey on Thursday as Unions NSW secretary, said AI had been a “trojan horse” measure – workers were told “this is going to make life more efficient for you, easier for you, but actually employers are bringing it in to roll out more work on an already highly leveraged workforce”.
Unions had in the past backed an outright ban on unpaid overtime but Mr Costa said this risked being a “blunt instrument”, and another option would be to use the award system to tackle the issue on an industry by industry basis.
“Definitely I think it would make a lot more sense to do it through the award system if you want to make sure that it’s industry appropriate and industry has a say in how it works,” he said.
“You could have a system where each award needs to consider the specific industry realities.
“Employers need overtime but workers cannot afford to do it for free.” Prior to being elected assistant secretary of Unions NSW in 2023, Mr Costa, 43, worked as an industrial officer and lawyer with the national offices of the Rail, Tram and Bus Industry Union and the Australian Workers Union.
Mr Costa said unions would continue pushing the Minns government to introduce a standalone labour hire licensing scheme, citing research showing how 63 labour hire operators banned in Queensland and Victoria were now trading in NSW.
Discussing the NSW state election next March and the prospects of One Nation, he said unions would be “getting out and telling the honest truth” to workers and ordinary Australians about the minor party.
“Yes, they’re coming out saying they are going to take on the establishment, but they’re not up to the job, they’re wreckers,” he said.
“I think most Australians think of Pauline Hanson as a bit of a whinger. She’s been around for 30 years. I was protesting against Pauline Hanson when I was in high school. She’s been saying the same thing since then. “She hates everything about Australia. She whinges about Australia constantly. She hates that we are multicultural. She hates that there are multi-lingual people in our country. She hates that we have minimum wages. She thinks workers are lazy.”
